A2.text:
Aysel is twenty-two. She lives with her parents and two younger brothers in a busy flat in Baku. There is always noise: the TV, music, phone calls and her brothers' games.

In August, her family went to the village for a week. Aysel had to stay in Baku because of her job. She was alone for the first time.

“Can you keep your own company for a whole week?” her mother asked on the phone.

“Of course,” Aysel laughed. “I am very independent.”

On the first evening, she loved the silence. She watched a film and ate pizza on the sofa. But on the second day, she felt lonely. The flat was too quiet. She missed her brothers' noise.

On the third day, she made a new routine. She went for a walk on the Boulevard every morning. In the evening, she read books and cooked simple meals. Sometimes she sat by the window, lost in thought.

Slowly, Aysel understood something. She was an introvert. Being alone helped her to recharge. She felt calm and happy.

On Sunday, her family came home. The flat was noisy again. Aysel hugged everyone. She was very happy to see them.

But now, every Sunday morning, she takes two hours of me time. She walks by the sea alone, and she enjoys her solitude.

questions.q: What does Aysel learn in the story?
options: She enjoys time alone and needs it to feel calm
She wants to live in the village
She does not like her brothers

questions.q: Why did Aysel stay in Baku?
options: She did not like the village
questions.why: “Aysel had to stay in Baku because of her job.”

questions.q: What did Aysel do every morning in her new routine?
questions.why: “She went for a walk on the Boulevard every morning.”

questions.q: Aysel felt lonely on the first evening.
questions.why: “On the first evening, she loved the silence.” She felt lonely on the second day.

questions.q: Aysel takes “me time” every Sunday. What is “me time”?
options: Time she spends alone, doing what she likes

questions.q: How does Aysel feel when her family comes home?
options: Happy, but she still wants some time alone
questions.why: She hugs everyone, but now she takes two hours alone every Sunday.

B1.text:
Aysel had never spent a single night alone. She shared a three-room flat in Ahmadli with her parents, her two teenage brothers and a grandmother who watched Turkish series at full volume. Silence, in that flat, was something that happened only between two and six in the morning.

So when her family left for her grandmother's village in Ismayilli for a week in August, and Aysel had to stay behind for work, everyone was worried — except Aysel.

“Will you be all right? Can you keep your own company for seven whole days?” her mother asked three times before getting into the car.

“Mum, I'm twenty-two. I'm perfectly independent.”

The first evening felt like a holiday. She ate pizza on the sofa, watched a film without anyone talking through it and went to bed in total silence. The second day was harder. The flat felt enormous and strangely cold. For the first time in her life, she felt genuinely lonely, and she missed even the noise she usually complained about.

On the third day, she decided to build a routine. She walked along the seafront every morning before work, cooked properly in the evenings and started reading the novels that had been sitting on her shelf for years. Some evenings she simply sat on the balcony, lost in thought, watching the lights come on across the city.

By Thursday, she noticed something surprising: she was sleeping better, thinking more clearly and feeling calmer than she had in months. She had always assumed she was just shy. Now she realised she was an introvert who needed solitude the way her phone needed a charger — to recharge.

When her family burst back in on Sunday, she hugged every one of them, grandmother included.

But the next week, she made an announcement at dinner. “Sunday mornings are my me time. Two hours. Nobody calls, nobody needs anything.”

Her brothers groaned. Her grandmother turned up the TV.

questions.q: What is the story mainly about?
options: Aysel's family moves to a village
A week alone helps Aysel understand that she needs solitude
questions.why: She realises she is an introvert who needs time alone to recharge.

questions.q: What did Aysel notice by Thursday?
options: She was sleeping better and feeling calmer
She had read all her books
questions.why: “...sleeping better, thinking more clearly and feeling calmer.”

questions.q: Aysel's mother asked her question only once.
Her mother asks, “Can you keep your own company?” What does she mean?
options: Can you start your own business?
Can you be happy alone, without other people?
questions.why: She is worried Aysel will feel lonely for seven days.

questions.q: What does the last line suggest?
options: The family will always respect Aysel's me time
The family's noise will continue as usual
The brothers are happy for her
questions.why: Her brothers groan and her grandmother turns up the TV.

B2.text:
In twenty-two years, Aysel had never spent a night alone. Home was a three-room flat in Ahmadli shared with her parents, two teenage brothers and a grandmother devoted to Turkish dramas at maximum volume. True silence, in that household, existed only between roughly two and six in the morning, and even then it was frequently interrupted by someone raiding the fridge.

So when the family decamped to her grandmother's village in Ismayilli for a week in August, leaving Aysel behind because she couldn't get time off work, the general mood was one of mild alarm — shared by everybody except Aysel.

“Are you sure you can keep your own company for seven whole days?” her mother asked, for the third time, with one foot already in the car.

“Mum. I'm twenty-two and entirely independent. Go.”

The first evening was pure luxury: pizza on the sofa, a film watched without commentary, a bed in absolute stillness. The second day was a different story. The flat seemed to have tripled in size overnight, and the quiet acquired a weight of its own. She found herself listening for a slammed door or a brother's shout, and with some astonishment recognised the feeling: she was lonely. She even missed the noise she had complained about her whole life.

On the third morning, she resolved to give the days a shape. She established a routine — an early walk along the seafront, proper cooking in the evenings, and finally opening the novels that had gathered dust on her shelf for years. Some nights she simply sat on the balcony, lost in thought, watching the city light up window by window.

By Thursday, something unexpected had happened. She was sleeping more deeply, thinking more clearly and feeling calmer than she could remember. She had always filed herself under “shy”; now she suspected the more accurate word was introvert — someone who needed solitude not as an escape but as a way to recharge.

When the family burst back through the door on Sunday, she embraced every one of them, grandmother included, with real joy.

Seven days later, she made an announcement over dinner. “From now on, Sunday mornings are my me time. Two hours. No calls, no errands, no exceptions.”

Her brothers groaned in unison. Her grandmother, without a word, reached for the remote and turned the volume up.

questions.q: What does Aysel discover about herself?
options: She is afraid of the dark
She is an introvert who needs solitude to recharge
questions.why: “...someone who needed solitude not as an escape but as a way to recharge.”

questions.q: Why did Aysel stay in Baku?
options: She couldn't get time off work
questions.why: “...because she couldn't get time off work.”

questions.q: What did Aysel feel on the second day?
questions.why: “...she recognised the feeling: she was lonely.”

questions.q: Aysel had always described herself as shy.
Aysel sat on the balcony “lost in thought”. What does this mean?
options: She was thinking deeply and didn't notice what was around her
questions.why: She was quietly thinking while watching the city.

questions.q: What is the tone of the ending?
options: Humorous — the family's habits won't change easily
questions.why: The brothers groan and the grandmother turns the TV up.
